about: A made-up inbox for scoring the email classifier. Every person, company and address is fictional. Gold labels follow the classifier's own definitions (classify.py INSTRUCTIONS). A list of values means any of them is acceptable; event_optional means a calendar entry is neither required nor penalised; urgent null means importance isn't scored for that case. replyExpected is whether the sender is waiting for the person to write back; a reply asked for only if something doesn't suit is false. 'evidence' is the text the right answer depends on, so the harness can tell when it was cut off before the model saw it. The long cases put it at every length the classifier might be cut to, from 600 characters to past 4,000. 'tags' group cases for a score of their own: confirm-by-reply is automated mail that asks for a written reply to confirm or cancel (replyExpected true), automated-no-reply is automated mail about a booking that confirms by a link or asks nothing (false).

cases.subject: Your final interview at Pademelon Labs
cases.body:
Hi Sam,

Thanks again for your time over the last few weeks. The team really enjoyed your technical interview, and we'd love you to come in for the final stage of our process for the Senior Test Automation Engineer role.

What happens at the final stage
The final stage is a half day at our office. It's the last step before we make a decision, and it's designed to be as close as possible to a normal afternoon on the team. You'll meet the people you'd be working with every day, see how we plan and ship work, and have plenty of time to ask questions. We know that interviews are a two-way street, and we want you to leave with a clear picture of whether Pademelon is the right place for you.

The afternoon has four parts:

1. Pairing session (90 minutes). You'll pair with one of our test automation engineers on a real (but non-sensitive) part of our codebase. We'll use our usual tools: Playwright, TypeScript and our in-house test runner. You can drive, navigate or swap; we care much more about how you think and communicate than about how much code you write. You're welcome to look things up, just as you would on a normal day.

2. Systems conversation (45 minutes). With a Staff Engineer, you'll talk through how you would test a system you've never seen before. We'll sketch the architecture of one of our services on a whiteboard and ask where you would focus, what you would automate and what you'd leave to exploratory testing.

3. Values interview (30 minutes). With someone from outside the engineering team, you'll talk about how you work with others, how you handle disagreement, and what you need from a team to do your best work.

4. Meet the team (30 minutes). An informal chat with a few people from the Quality team over afternoon tea. This part isn't assessed.

How to prepare
You don't need to study anything in particular. If you'd like to get a feel for our work, our engineering blog has posts on how we run our test suites in parallel and how we decide which tests to keep. It might also help to think of a couple of examples from your own work: a bug you're proud of finding, a test suite you improved, or a time you disagreed with a decision and how it played out.

Our office
We're at Level 3, 18 Wattle Lane, Surry Hills. The nearest train station is Central, about a ten-minute walk away, and several bus routes stop on Crown Street. There's bike parking in the basement and showers on Level 1 if you're riding in. The building has step-free access from the Wattle Lane entrance and lifts to every floor.

Travel and expenses
If you're travelling from outside Sydney, we'll cover reasonable travel costs. Keep your receipts and our team will reimburse you within two weeks.

Adjustments
If you need any adjustments to take part, such as a different start time, extra breaks, a screen reader or an interpreter, please let us know through your candidate portal. You don't need to tell us why.

Your privacy
We collect and store the information you give us during the recruitment process to assess your application. We keep it for twelve months after the process ends, unless you ask us to delete it sooner. You can read our full candidate privacy notice in the portal.

Your final interview
Tuesday 20 October, 1:00pm to 4:30pm (AEDT)
Pademelon Labs, Level 3, 18 Wattle Lane, Surry Hills
Ask for Hannah at reception.

If anything changes, you can reschedule through the candidate portal.

See you soon,
The Pademelon Labs Recruiting Team

Hi Sam,

Your interview for the Platform QA Engineer role at Ironbark Energy has been confirmed. This email has everything you need to know, so please read it through and keep it handy.

About Ironbark Energy
Ironbark Energy supplies electricity and gas to more than 1.2 million homes and businesses across Australia, and we're building the platforms that will help our customers move to solar, batteries and electric vehicles. Our Platform team runs the systems that bill our customers, read their meters and keep their accounts up to date: around 400 services, deployed hundreds of times a week.

Why Ironbark
- Hybrid working: most of our engineers come into the office two days a week.
- Sixteen weeks of paid parental leave for every parent, from day one.
- A learning budget of $2,000 a year, plus time to use it.
- Discounted energy plans for you and your household.
- Volunteer leave, wellbeing leave and the option to buy extra annual leave.

Diversity and inclusion
We want our teams to reflect the communities we serve. We welcome applications from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, people with disability, people from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds and people of all ages, genders and sexualities. If there's anything we can do to make our process work better for you, tell us.

About your interview
This is a 60-minute video interview with two people from the Platform team: an Engineering Manager and a Senior QA Engineer. It has three parts.

First, we'll talk about your experience. We'll ask you to walk us through a recent project and the testing you did on it, and we'll ask follow-up questions about the choices you made.

Second, a scenario. We'll describe a change to one of our billing services and ask how you'd make sure it was safe to release. There's no single right answer: we're interested in the questions you ask, the risks you notice and how you'd balance speed against confidence.

Third, your questions. We'll leave at least ten minutes at the end for anything you'd like to ask us about the role, the team or Ironbark.

Technical requirements
The interview will be held on Zoom. You can join from a laptop or desktop computer using the Zoom app or a browser. We don't recommend joining from a phone, as you may be asked to share your screen. Please check that:
- your internet connection is stable (a wired connection is best if you have one);
- your camera and microphone work, and that you've allowed your browser to use them;
- you're somewhere quiet where you won't be interrupted for an hour.
If your connection drops during the interview, rejoin using the same link. If you can't rejoin within five minutes, we'll call you on the phone number in your application.

Tips from our team
- Use real examples. We'd rather hear about something that went wrong and what you learned than a perfect story.
- Think out loud. In the scenario, we're more interested in how you get to an answer than in the answer itself.
- It's fine to pause, ask us to repeat a question or take a moment to think.
- Have a glass of water and something to write on nearby.

Frequently asked questions
Do I need to prepare anything? No presentation or test is needed. You might like to read about our Platform team on the Ironbark careers site.
What should I wear? Whatever you're comfortable in. Most of our team dress casually.
Who will I be speaking with? You'll get the names of your interviewers in a separate email the day before.
When will I hear back? We aim to let every candidate know the outcome within five working days of their interview.
Can I bring a support person? Yes. Let us know in the candidate portal and we'll add them to the invitation.

Your privacy
Ironbark Energy collects your personal information to assess your suitability for this role and for similar roles in the future. Your information is stored securely by our recruitment platform, Workwise, and is only shared with the people involved in hiring for this role. You can ask to see, correct or delete your information at any time through the candidate portal. Our full privacy policy is on our website.

Need to reschedule? Use the link in your candidate portal at least 24 hours before your interview.

Good luck, Sam. We're looking forward to meeting you.

Ironbark Energy Talent Team

cases.subject: The Test Bench #87: flaky tests, contract testing and an October meetup
cases.body:
The Test Bench, issue 87

Hello testers,

Spring is here, the builds are green (mostly), and this issue is a big one. We've got a deep dive on flaky tests, a reader's story about moving a team to contract testing, the tools we've been trying this month, and a few dates for your diary.

Sydney meetup
Our next Sydney meetup is on Wednesday 14 October at 6pm, hosted by a software studio in Pyrmont. Two talks: one on testing event-driven systems, and one on what the speaker learned running exploratory testing sessions with customer support staff. Pizza and drinks from 5:30pm. Spots are limited, so RSVP on the meetup page.

Deep dive: where flaky tests come from
Every team has them: the tests that pass on your machine, fail in CI, and pass again when you hit retry. This month we went through 300 flaky tests that readers sent us and sorted them by cause. The biggest group, about 40 per cent, came down to timing: a test that waits a fixed number of milliseconds for something that usually, but not always, happens in time. The next biggest group was shared state, where one test leaves data behind that another test trips over, usually only when they run in a particular order or in parallel. Then came the network: tests that call a real service that is sometimes slow or down. The smallest group, but the most painful to find, was tests that depend on the clock: the date, the time zone, or a daylight saving change.

Our advice is boring but it works. Replace fixed waits with waiting for a condition. Give every test its own data. Fake the network at the boundary. Inject the clock. And when a test does flake, record it, because a flaky test you've written down is a bug report, and a flaky test you've retried is a secret.

Early-bird tickets for TestCon close on Friday 16 October. After that the price goes up by $150, so if you've been meaning to ask your manager, now's the time.

Reader story: contract testing at a mid-sized retailer
A reader who leads testing at an online retailer wrote in about moving her team from a large end-to-end suite to consumer-driven contract tests. The end-to-end suite took 90 minutes, failed about one run in four for reasons nobody could explain, and had stopped catching real bugs. Over six months the team replaced most of it with contract tests between their twelve services and a much smaller set of end-to-end journeys for the paths that make money. Build times dropped to 15 minutes, and the team says they trust a red build again. Her advice: start with the service that breaks most often, get one contract working end to end, and only then roll it out.

Tools we tried this month
- A snapshot testing plugin that finally handles dates sensibly.
- A command-line tool that reruns only the tests affected by your change.
- A browser extension that records your exploratory session as notes and screenshots.
We'll write up all three properly in the next issue.

Free webinar: testing with AI agents
On Tuesday 20 October at 12pm AEDT, we're hosting a free one-hour webinar on using AI agents to write and maintain tests: what works, what doesn't, and how to review what they produce. Register on our website and we'll send you the recording if you can't make it live.

cases.subject: Pytestify 5.0 is out
cases.body:
Pytestify 5.0 is out

This is our biggest release in three years. Here's what's new, what's changed and what you need to do before you upgrade.

What's new
- Parallel fixtures by default. Session-scoped fixtures are now shared safely across workers, so most suites can drop their own locking code.
- A new results format. Every run can now write a single JSON file with each test's outcome, timing and labels, ready for dashboards.
- Faster collection. Large suites collect up to three times faster, thanks to a rewritten import cache.
- Better failure messages for nested data: diffs now show only the keys that changed.

Breaking changes
- Python 3.9 is no longer supported. Pytestify 5.0 needs Python 3.10 or later.
- The old --legacy-report flag has been removed. Use the new results format instead.
- Fixtures that yield more than once now raise an error rather than a warning.

Support for 4.x
We'll keep fixing security issues in the 4.x series until 31 March 2027. After that, 4.x will no longer receive updates of any kind. Python 3.9 users should plan their move to 3.10 before then.

Migration webinar
Our maintainers are running a free migration webinar on Tuesday 13 October at 10am AEDT. We'll walk through upgrading a real project from 4.2 to 5.0, including the breaking changes above, and answer questions live. The recording will be on our blog afterwards.

Upgrading
pip install --upgrade pytestify
Then run your suite with -W error::DeprecationWarning to catch anything that will break in the next release.

Thank you to the 112 people who contributed to this release, and to everyone who tested the betas.

The Pytestify maintainers
